posts.text: One mental model I find particularly useful in client conversations is to treat AI governance as an extension of the enterprise control environment — not as a separate compliance layer. I usually start with the business use cases and work downward: What AI systems, models, copilots and agents are actually being used? What data do they access? What risks do they introduce? And what controls should apply based on that risk? But an equally important step is understanding what the organization already has. Most enterprises are not starting from zero. They already have investments across data governance, IAM, cybersecurity, privacy, SDLC, GRC, vendor risk, logging and monitoring. Many of the controls required for AI already exist somewhere in that environment. The practical governance work is therefore often about connecting the pieces: Business use case → AI inventory → risk tiering → control requirements → existing controls → gap analysis → control design. From there, the gaps can be addressed through the right combination of process, architecture and technology — rather than automatically creating another governance layer or buying another tool. The final piece is becoming increasingly important in my work around agentic AI: continuous assurance. As AI systems become more dynamic and autonomous, governance cannot rely exclusively on what was assessed at intake or deployment. For higher-risk systems, we increasingly need evidence from the operating environment itself: observe, detect, escalate, remediate and document. This model helps me keep client conversations grounded in a simple question: How do we build on what is already working, close the material gaps, and make AI governance operational, measurable and scalable? posts.text: 🚀 End-to-End Generative AI Production Architecture Building a GenAI application is not just about connecting an LLM to a chatbot. A production-ready AI system needs the right architecture across data, models, orchestration, security, deployment, and monitoring. Here’s a high-level view 👇 🔹 1. Application & API Layer Users interact through web/mobile apps, while APIs handle requests, authentication, and rate limits. 🔹 2. Data Ingestion & Preparation Documents, PDFs, websites, databases, and other sources are processed, cleaned, chunked, and converted into embeddings. 🔹 3. AI Orchestration Frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, or AutoGen can manage agents, tools, RAG pipelines, memory, and workflows. 🔹 4. LLM Layer Models such as GPT, Claude, Gemini, or Llama handle generation, reasoning, summarization, coding, and more. 🔹 5. RAG & Vector Database Relevant knowledge can be retrieved from vector databases such as Pinecone, FAISS, or Chroma before generating an answer. 🔹 6. Infrastructure & Deployment Cloud platforms, containers, Kubernetes, CI/CD, and autoscaling help move AI applications from development to production. 🔹 7. Security & Observability Production AI needs authentication, access control, encryption, guardrails, logging, tracing, metrics, and alerts. 🔹 8. Monitoring & Optimization Track latency, token usage, costs, errors, model performance, and user feedback to continuously improve the system. 💡 Key takeaway: A successful GenAI product is not just LLM + Prompt. It is: Data + RAG + Orchestration + LLM + Infrastructure + Security + Monitoring That’s what turns an AI prototype into a scalable, secure, and reliable production system. 🚀 What layer do you think is the most challenging to build for production AI? 🎯 Follow Virat Radadiya 🟢 for more..... hashtag #GenerativeAI hashtag #AIEngineering hashtag #LLM hashtag #RAG hashtag #AIArchitecture hashtag #LangGraph hashtag #MachineLearning hashtag #AIAgents hashtag #CloudComputing hashtag #SoftwareEngineering hashtag #MLOps hashtag #GenAI

posts.text: Right, show me some love and sign up to hear me bang on about AI implementation and process redesign on a panel for an hour. Camunda has just published research surveying 1,000 process decision-makers and 5,000 employees about what happens when AI meets the processes organisations actually run. 78% say their organisation needs to fundamentally redesign its processes rather than layer AI on top of them to remain competitive. 79% say bolting AI onto existing processes creates less internal resistance than redesigning them completely. That's almost the AI implementation problem in two statistics. They know they need to redesign, but the path of least organisational resistance is to do exactly the opposite. Another finding interests me even more: 75% of process decision-makers say trying to implement AI has shone a light on broken processes in their organisation. Implementation isn't just where we execute organisational design, it's one of the ways we discover what needs designing. Put AI into real work and you start discovering assumptions, dependencies, exceptions, hand-offs and coordination requirements that weren't necessarily visible beforehand. Which is why I don't think the answer is simply to design the perfect new process and then implement it. Implementation isn't just execution, it's discovery. Camunda asked me to join Ritu Jyoti on September 29th to dig into their research and talk about what all this means for AI implementation, process redesign and how work changes when intelligent systems become part of it. posts.text: This man is demonstrating Agentic AI without using AI. Yes. You read that right. I captured this video of a person painting a four-storey building using nothing but a rope. Watch his movements carefully. He has a goal. He understands the environment. He continuously adjusts his position. He makes decisions based on the situation. And he takes action to complete the task. There is no robot. No LLM. No automation framework. No GPU. Yet, there is something remarkably similar to what we are trying to build with Agentic AI. Goal → Observe → Decide → Act → Adjust → Repeat. That is the essence of an intelligent system. The fascinating part? From a distance, his movements almost look like a poem being written on a four-storey wall. Every movement matters. Every stroke has a purpose. The rope is his tool. The wall is his canvas. And his intelligence is in how he uses the tool to accomplish the goal. We sometimes think making a system “intelligent” means adding more AI. Maybe not. Intelligence is not about how many tools you have. It is about how effectively you can use the tools you have to achieve an objective. That is exactly the mindset we need when building Agentic AI systems. Don’t start with: “Where can I add an LLM?” Start with: “What is the goal? What does the system need to observe? What decisions does it need to make? What actions can it take? How does it learn from the outcome?” The technology may be new. The idea of intelligence isn’t. hashtag #AgenticAI hashtag #ArtificialIntelligence hashtag #AI hashtag #IntelligentSystems hashtag #Innovation hashtag #HumanIngenuity hashtag #AIEngineering hashtag #FutureOfAI

posts.text: A powerful model is only the beginning. Enterprise AI creates value when strategy, data, architecture, governance, and execution work as one system. Buying an LLM will not create that system. An enterprise AI foundation needs four connected layers: → Strategy and Readiness Start with a business problem. Confirm the data is usable, secure ownership, prioritize use cases, define ROI, and decide where to build or buy. → Core AI Architecture Connect trusted data. Use RAG for grounded responses, agents for multi-step workflows, and human review for sensitive decisions. Add memory, orchestration, APIs, evaluation, and observability. → Governance and Controls Define who can access what. Protect sensitive data, apply guardrails, test security, maintain audit trails, monitor model behavior, and manage the AI lifecycle. → Platforms and Tools Microsoft Foundry, AWS Bedrock, Vertex AI, Databricks, Snowflake, ServiceNow, and agent frameworks can speed up delivery. But tools cannot replace a clear operating model. The advantage comes from connecting every layer. Strategy gives AI a purpose. Architecture makes it usable. Governance makes it trustworthy. Platforms make it scalable. That is the difference between an impressive AI demo and a capability people can rely on every day. Where is your organization strongest today: strategy, architecture, governance, or execution?

posts.text: After assessing hundreds of AI use cases and controls and designing governance for production ready agentic AI - I have become convinced that the AI movement will create organisational functions most businesses have not yet contemplated or planned for. Not more prompt engineers. Not more data scientists. But new leaders for a workforce that is no longer entirely human. The Head of People role may need to become the Head of People and Virtual Agents. Why? Because once an AI agent has a defined role, access to enterprise systems and information, delegated authority and the ability to take action, it is no longer merely a technology tool or an assistant. It is a workforce participant. Not a person. Not an employee. But a participant that can influence customer outcomes, make recommendations, trigger workflows, access sensitive data and operate at a speed no manager can directly supervise. That will force uncomfortable questions and ones I ask on a daily basis: - Who is accountable for an agent’s decisions? - What work should never be delegated? - When an agent fails, who is responsible: the manager, process owner, platform owner or executive who approved the design? (or no one). - If a virtual workforce creates extraordinary productivity, who gets the bonuses? Other functions I expect to emerge or rapidly expand are: People and Virtual Agents Designing the human-agent workforce, work allocation, capability, supervision and accountability. Virtual Workforce and Identity Governance Ensuring every agent has an owner, purpose, permissions, financial limits, audit trail, kill switch and retirement process. AI Robustness Testing — continuously determining whether agents fail safely when given edge-case and out of bounds scenarios. AI Red Teaming and Adversarial Testing: Deliberately and continuously trying to manipulate agents into leaking data, bypassing controls, misusing tools or taking harmful actions. The future workforce plan will not ask only: “How many FTE do we need?” It will ask: "What is the right mix of people, virtual agents and delegated authority—and who governs it?” My provocation: organisations that are tool obsessed and not actively pivoting their operating model, workforce strategy, identity controls and risk governance around this shift are asleep at the wheel. What are others noticing across the industry?

posts.text: Open-source maintenance gets messy fast. This repo puts guardrails before AI agents. Hive is an open-source AI agent orchestration project for teams maintaining GitHub-based open-source projects. It helps you move issues and PRs through an agent workflow by classifying work before it reaches an LLM, then adjusting agent cadences to the queue depth. Key features: • GitHub work triage – enumerates issues and PRs, then classifies them by complexity • Deterministic pipeline – handles filtering, classification, merge-gating, and enforcement before agent judgment calls • Multiple agent backends – supports Claude, Copilot, Gemini, and Goose for code-reading, fixes, and PR work • Queue-aware governor – switches between surge, busy, quiet, and idle modes with different agent cadences • Configurable autonomy – ACMM levels define whether agents advise, file issues, open hold-gated PRs, or auto-merge on green CI It’s open-source (Apache License 2.0). 🔗 GitHub: https://lnkd.in/dnWKmA-t ⸻ ♻️ Share this with your network if you found it useful or insightful. ✉️ If you’re into AI, ML, agents, and building real systems, join my newsletter (it’s free): dankornas.substack.com

posts.text: The best AI governance advice I've ever gotten had nothing to do with AI. I gave a keynote on wednesday Deutsche Telekom IoT and, like I always do, asked the people who reached out afterward one question: what stuck with you? I love asking this. We all have selective hearing, everyone walks out of the same talk having heard a different talk. Watching what actually lands tells me more than any applause does. This time, one thing came up again and again. Not the framework I built the whole keynote around. A single reframe on AI governance I almost mentioned in passing 😉 Here it is: Stop asking cross-functional teams to approve AI use cases. Ask them to assess the risk relevant to their function instead. Legal isn't comfortable "approving" an AI use case. Security isn't either. Compliance isn't either. That's not what they're trained to do, and asking them to do it is exactly why governance stalls, everyone hedges, nobody wants to be the name on the sign-off when something goes wrong. But ask them to assess risk within their own domain? That, they can do all day. It's their actual expertise. The approval itself belongs somewhere else entirely: with the business owner. They own the outcome. They own the consequences. So they're the ones who should decide the acceptable risk level and the mitigations, informed by what legal, security, and compliance found, not blocked by it. Assess vs. approve. Different roles, different people, and suddenly governance stops being the thing that quietly kills every AI initiative. I learned this from my joint projects with Naureen and it's a small sentence that has changed how I advise every executive team I work with since. Sometimes the biggest takeaway from a Keynote isn't the big idea. It's the one operational sentence someone can use on Monday morning or the one we put into practice with our clients at scailers. What's a reframe like this that changed how you work?

posts.text: Built an AI multi-agent travel planner — and made sure the AI never touches the math. Most "AI trip planner" demos let the LLM eyeball a budget and hope for the best. I wanted something closer to production-grade: an agent pipeline where the model reasons, but never computes. Here's how it works: 🔹 A coordinator (plain Python, not an LLM router) drives a deterministic pipeline — no black-box orchestration 🔹 Flight, hotel & activity agents research in parallel via Google ADK 🔹 A selector agent proposes an itinerary → a pure-Python budget engine checks it → if it's over budget, the loop forces the agent to trade down and try again — automatically, until it fits or hits an iteration cap 🔹 Every agent's decision is logged to a trace panel on the Next.js frontend, so the reasoning is inspectable, not guessed.... The interesting engineering problem wasn't "call an LLM" — it was designing the boundary between what the model decides and what deterministic code verifies. The LLM ranks and justifies; a calculate_budget() function owns every dollar figure. Wired in real providers too — SerpApi & Sky Scrapper for flights, Hotelbeds for hotels, Tavily for live activity data (with a Gemini classifier assigning price tiers, never raw prices) — all behind a Protocol-based interface with a mock dataset as a zero-cost fallback, so the whole system degrades gracefully instead of breaking when an API hiccups. posts.text: AI transformation is not primarily a technology transformation. It is an operating model transformation. Many enterprises begin with models, copilots and agents. But the real shift happens when AI changes how work is executed, who decides and how governance operates. Deploying AI without redesigning the operating model often creates limited value: faster tasks, but the same bottlenecks, approval chains, silos and governance friction. The deeper shift is from: Human executes. System supports. to: Human governs. AI executes within defined boundaries. This changes the enterprise itself. 1. Work becomes human + agent work AI agents can retrieve context, reason, invoke tools, coordinate workflows, validate outcomes and escalate exceptions. Work must be redesigned around people and digital actors. 2. Decision rights become an architecture concern The question is not only “Which model should we use?” It is “Who is authorized to make which decision?” Enterprises need explicit boundaries across Recommend, Assist, Execute, Decide and Govern. 3. Governance moves into the execution path Manual review boards cannot scale to millions of AI-driven actions. Policies, risk thresholds, security controls and approval rules must become machine-enforceable through Policy-as-Code, Architecture-as-Code and Decision-Rights-as-Code. 4. Roles evolve Architects, engineers, SREs and product owners will spend less time on repetitive execution and more time defining intent, guardrails, policies, exceptions and outcomes. 5. Autonomy becomes a managed variable Not every process should be autonomous. Enterprises need levels from manual execution to assist, recommend, act-with-approval and bounded autonomy. The level should depend on risk and blast radius. 6. Enterprise Architecture becomes more important AI introduces models, agents, tools, memory, knowledge and platforms. Without discipline, organizations risk agent sprawl, duplicated capabilities and rising cost. Transformation should start with business outcomes, capabilities, value streams and decision architecture before jumping to AI platforms. A strong AI operating model connects: Strategy → Capabilities → Decisions → Human/Agent Responsibilities → Governance → Data → Platforms → Automation → Observability → Continuous Improvement. The goal is not to deploy the maximum number of agents. The goal is to create a more adaptive enterprise where humans retain accountability while AI accelerates execution safely and economically. The strategic question is no longer: “Where can we use AI?” It is: “How should our enterprise operate when intelligent agents become participants in work, decisions and execution?” That is AI transformation. hashtag #AI hashtag #AINative hashtag #AIEngineering hashtag #AgenticAI hashtag #GenAI hashtag #AIReasoning hashtag #EnterpriseArchitecture hashtag #OperatingModel hashtag #DigitalTransformation hashtag #AIGovernance hashtag #Automation hashtag #AgentOps hashtag #EngineeringLeadership hashtag #AITransformation hashtag #FutureReady hashtag #AIReadiness

posts.text: Who is in the loop? Language shapes how we design reality. I have been working a lot on process reengineering for effective AI adoption lately. What I see is that some terms create confusion that complicates the implementation. When we say "Artificial Intelligence" instead of "Language Model", we create expectations. I already have cases where a client expected AI to "implement itself somehow". As a result, they didn't allocate the right resources for the project, and implementation failed. When we say "Human in the Loop"... Think about what that phrase implies. There is already a “loop” - apparently belonging to the machine - and now we insert a human into it. Shouldn't it often be AI in the human loop? Or simply: AI in the workflow. This isn't just semantics. It creates a different design focus. If I start with Human in the Loop, the architecture can easily become: AI acts → human checks. But if I start with the business process and the human task, the logic becomes: Business goal → human work → AI support where useful → human judgment and accountability. That is a fundamentally different approach to AI transformation. So perhaps one of the first questions in AI-enabled process redesign should not be: Where do we put the human in the loop? But: What is the job to be done, what is the right process for doing it — and where should AI fit into that process? And then, perhaps, the even more uncomfortable question: Whose loop is it in the first place? hashtag #HumanCenteredAI hashtag #AITransformation hashtag #ProcessReengineering hashtag #HumanAIInteraction hashtag #AIGovernance

posts.text: An LLM is not an AI agent. It becomes agentic when the system around it can understand goals, plan work, use tools, remember context, act, and recover from failure. Here are the 10 building blocks: → Foundation Model Provides reasoning, generation, understanding, and tool calling. → Agent Orchestration Routes tasks, manages workflows, maintains state, and handles retries. → Context and Instructions Defines goals, rules, requirements, task context, and tools. → Memory and State Retains conversation history, preferences, progress, and knowledge. → Knowledge and RAG Retrieves trusted information and grounds responses. → Tools and Actions Calls APIs, queries databases, executes code, and triggers actions. → Planning and Workflow Breaks complex goals into tasks, sequences them, and tracks progress. → Multi-Agent Collaboration Lets specialized agents delegate, hand off, and coordinate work. → Security and Guardrails Controls identity, permissions, tool access, filtering, and approval. → Observability and Evaluation Tracks quality, cost, tool calls, failures, and performance. A strong model can produce a good answer. A strong agentic system can complete useful work safely and repeatedly. The advantage will not come from choosing one model. It will come from designing the system around it. Which building block is your team prioritizing? BTW, pre-order for the book is now open! posts.text: AI should not handle everything. The enterprise AI decision is knowing what to automate, what to augment, and what should remain human. Before selecting a tool, start with the process: → Is it repetitive and high-volume? → Are the inputs structured and rules clear? → Is the work based on text, documents, or emails? → Does it involve sensitive data? → Does it require judgment or empathy? → Could a mistake create legal, financial, or safety risks? → Would automation save enough time? Clear rules and structured inputs may be ready for automation. Unstructured work may need GenAI. Sensitive workflows require guardrails. High-risk decisions should stay human-led, while AI assists with drafting. Only then should you choose the platform. → ServiceNow for tickets, approvals, employee workflows, and knowledge. → UiPath or Automation Anywhere for legacy applications. → Power Automate, Zapier, or n8n for simple team workflows. → Salesforce Agentforce or Zendesk AI for customer-facing processes. → Integration Hub for synchronizing data across systems. → Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, or Vertex AI for custom applications. → Power BI or Tableau for analytics and dashboards. The goal is not to put AI everywhere. It is to place the right level of automation inside the right process, with the right controls and human oversight. What process inside your enterprise would you evaluate first?
